text.p: Reuters Holdings Plc chairman Sir Christopher Hogg said on Monday the company's principal market was enormous and still growing and that the company was wary of making "ill-judged acquisitions".
"...The global financial industry, Reuters principal market, is enormous and should be on a rising trend for many years to come," Hogg wrote in the company's annual report, published on Monday.
"The robust defence of our existing market positions and the exploitation of the many opportunities still open to us in this industry are therefore management's main priorities," he added.

"The main risks seem to us to be that we could be deflected by ill-judged acquisitions; or we could respond inadequately to the ever-rising tide of competition; or we could be outflanked by others who use evolving technology better."
Hogg said that Reuters still believed in returning excess cash to shareholders if an effective mechanism could be found.
"We have long deemed it wise to return to shareholders funds judged to be excess to the needs of the business," he said.
"We still take this view and the discussion currently is less about this end than about the best means of achieving it."

Reuters had net funds of 1.05 billion pounds ($1.7 billion) at the end of 1996. Plans to return 613 million stg to shareholders via a share buyback and special dividend were thwarted last year by a change in UK tax regulations.
Chief executive Peter Job said that the boom in technology and the development of the Internet would not undermine global news and information group Reuters.
Job said it was a good thing that people should be asking questions about Reuters role in the future.
"These very people will prove to be avid users of our information when they find out that we are still the best place to go (albeit at a cost) to get data fully accurately and fast," Job wrote.

"Competition is fierce. But with the right combination of open technologies and unique breadth of data and service, we shall have nothing to fear but complacency and lack of concentration," he added. ($ = 0.624 British Pounds)
